title: Critical Reasoning — Strengthen and Weaken Arguments
tagline: Year 3 — Premises, conclusions, hidden assumptions and the evidence that supports or undermines them

introduction.overview: A critical-reasoning question gives a short argument: some evidence (premises) leading to a conclusion. You are asked which new fact would make the conclusion more likely (strengthen), less likely (weaken), or which unstated belief the argument needs (assumption). The skill is to find the gap between premise and conclusion, because strengthening fills the gap and weakening opens it wider.
introduction.placementRelevance: Critical-reasoning items are a standard element of the reasoning sections in company and management tests.
introduction.realWorldContext: Evaluating a business case, a policy proposal or a news claim requires the same moves.

learningObjectives: Strengthen by closing the gap or ruling out alternatives
Weaken by offering another explanation or breaking the link
Identify necessary assumptions with the negation test

requiredTopics: Assumptions, Inferences, and Courses of Action
prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: An argument is a conclusion supported by premises. Strong arguments have premises that make the conclusion likely.

coreDefinitions: Premise: a stated reason or evidence.
Conclusion: the claim the premises are meant to support.
Assumption: an unstated link that must hold for the premises to support the conclusion.
Strengthener: new information that makes the conclusion more likely, often by ruling out an alternative cause.
Weakener: new information that makes the conclusion less likely, often by offering an alternative cause.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Every argument has a gap. Strengtheners cover the gap; weakeners dig it deeper. Ask: what else could explain the evidence?
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Mark the conclusion, mark the evidence, and state the gap in one line ("assumes that…"). Then test each option against the gap.

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Causal pattern
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: A then B ⇒ A caused B

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Strengthen
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Rule out alternatives or add direct evidence

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Weaken
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Give an alternative cause or break the link

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Assumption test
importantRulesAndFormulas.formula: Negate it; the argument should collapse

importantRulesAndFormulas.title: Scope
importantRulesAndFormulas.simpleExample: All accidents are caused by speed

mainNarrative: Take the argument: a company says its training programme raised productivity because output per employee in the trained department rose by 15%. The gap is that the rise may have happened anyway. A strengthener closes it: "Output in a similar department that did not take the programme stayed unchanged." That rules out the alternative that output rose for general reasons.
A weakener opens the gap: "A festival season started the same week and sales rose in all shops in the area" gives another explanation for a shop's rising sales.

For an assumption question, state what the argument needs. "The government plans to raise the speeding fine to reduce accidents" needs "Drivers will slow down to avoid the higher fine." Negate it and the plan fails. "All accidents are caused by speeding" is too strong: the plan needs only that some accidents are.

Correlation arguments are open to reverse causation. People who own pets report being happier. The columnist concludes that pets make people happier. A weakener: "People who are already happy are more likely to adopt and keep pets."
The best strengthener for a causal claim is usually a controlled comparison: an experiment where randomly assigned groups differ only in the factor claimed to matter.

deepDiveAspects.title: Alternative explanations
deepDiveAspects.content: When the premise is an observed change, the usual weakeners are another cause, a coincidence, or a change in how things were measured.

deepDiveAspects.title: Necessary vs sufficient
deepDiveAspects.content: An assumption is necessary for the argument; it need not be sufficient to prove it.

solvedExamples.title: Strengthen
solvedExamples.question: A company says its training programme improved productivity because output rose 15% in the trained department. Which fact strengthens this most?

steps.title: Strengthener
steps.explanation: A similar untrained department stayed unchanged.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: A similar department without the programme showed no rise in output
solvedExamples.whyItWorks: It rules out a general cause.

solvedExamples.title: Weaken
solvedExamples.question: A shop says its loyalty scheme raised sales because sales rose after it began. Which fact weakens this most?

steps.title: Gap
steps.explanation: Something else may have raised sales.

steps.title: Weakener
steps.explanation: A festival season started that week and all shops saw sales rise.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: A festival season began the same week and sales rose at all shops in the area

solvedExamples.title: Assumption
solvedExamples.question: To reduce accidents the government raises the fine for speeding. Which assumption does the plan depend on?

steps.title: Needed
steps.explanation: Drivers must slow down because of the higher fine.

steps.title: Negate
steps.explanation: If drivers do not slow down, the plan fails.

solvedExamples.finalAnswer: Drivers will slow down to avoid the higher fine
solvedExamples.commonTrap: Choosing "all accidents are caused by speeding".

traditionalVsShortcut.traditionalMethod: Pick the option that sounds related.
traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: State the gap, then pick the option that closes it (strengthen), widens it (weaken), or is needed to cross it (assumption).

commonMistakes.mistake: Choosing an option that only repeats the premise
commonMistakes.howToAvoid: The option must change the likelihood of the conclusion.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Discard options that are irrelevant to the link from premise to conclusion.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Always state the gap before reading the options.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Wrong options often mention the topic but not the link.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I weaken a causal claim?
Can I find a necessary assumption?
